newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-TIGER ADDS OOMPH TO MASTERS SCENE.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-TIGER ADDS OOMPH TO MASTERS SCENE.

text.p: The golf world returned to the scene of the disaster Monday but the big buzz around the grounds of cherished Augusta National did not involve Nick Faldo or Greg Norman, stars of last year's excruciating crash.
Tigermania swept through the galleries at the first practice day for the Masters and for one day at least, Tiger Woods reigned at Augusta.

Faldo, who won his third Masters last year as the swashbuckling Norman buckled in the final-round and squandered a six-stroke lead, bustled through the business of preparing for another assault on a major.
Norman lay low, dodging the limelight and practice-round hubbub ahead of Thursday's first round of the season's opening grand slam tournament.
Woods, the wunderkind whose power golf game has brought the tiger out in the fans, was the main attraction as far as the jam-packed, boisterous practice-day crowds were concerned.

The 21-year-old American, the winner of three successive U.S. Amateur crowns and three of the first nine tournaments he played once he turned pro on the U.S. tour, caused a sensation at the driving range when he showed up in late afternoon.
A stampede then followed him to the pitching area before his entourage of six security guards escorted him to the practice putting green, which went from placid to pulsating in the span of a minute.

Woods parted a sea of spectators to reach the first tee. There, teeing off alone, he gave the mob a glimpse of greatness as he launched a prodigious drive into a stiff wind. The ball carried some 40 yards beyond the distant bunker guarding the right side of the fairway.
The crowd roared and Woods, hoping to become the youngest Masters champion ever, wore a big smile as he strode off.
Smiles were stifled last year in the wake of Norman's stunning collapse when Faldo and the Australian waged a Masters Sunday for the ages -- but not for the squeamish.
Norman's final round of six-over-par 78 was like slow-motion torture and obscured the brilliant play of Faldo, who fired a day's-best 67 to produce an incredible 11-shot swing.
Faldo, who consoled Norman with a warm hug in an emotionally charged scene on the 72nd hole, says his round that Sunday "ranks as one of the greatest I've ever had."
Norman says: "It was all my fault. It wasn't anybody else's fault. I accept my responsibilities and fate."
But all that seemed like ancient history to Monday's practice day crowds, feeding off the energy of young Wood's potential.
Woods, who is 11 over par in six rounds played in two Masters as an amateur, also believes this year's tournament will provide him with a fresh start.
"The last two years I've had to take (college) finals the week before I arrived at Augusta. That's kind of tough on you. That's a pretty big disadvantage.

"And now that I'm a pro, I don't have that worry on my mind. I'm just playing, practicing whenever I want, and all the things I want. Therefore, I feel I'll be more prepared going into the tournament."
There are a host of other likely contenders and other stirring story lines at this year's Masters.

Jose Maria Olazabal, the 1994 Masters champion, is returning to Augusta National after being sidelined 18 months due to injury. The 31-year-old Spaniard last month won the Turespana Masters in the Canary Islands for an uplifting triumph.
"It is much better being here than watching on television," said Olazabal after Monday's practice.
Arnold Palmer, recovering from surgery for prostate cancer, will be competing in his 43rd consecutive Masters. the 67-year-old Palmer is one appearance shy of Sam Snead's record.
The stage could be set for a major championship breakthrough for one of the game's most deserving -- say a Davis Love III or Colin Montgomery of Britain.
But the fans' choice for best story would probably be Tiger Woods taking the next big step in his professional life.
